findings.where: H.4 layer 1 (sandbox jail) and layer 7; H.11 LI1 and LI7; E.2 Lanes group
findings.problem: The revised jail adds a private /tmp and /dev/shm, hides /run/user/<uid> and drops capabilities. It still shares the host PID namespace and says nothing about /proc, /sys or the environment. The build jail of N.8 has --unshare-pid for exactly this reason ('nothing outside can be killed'); the sandbox jail does not. (1) Without a PID namespace a jailed process can signal every aurnab process: kill needs no /proc, and nvidia-smi inside the jail prints the experiment worker's host PID. (2) A /proc mounted without a new PID namespace exposes /proc/<pid>/cwd, /root and /fd/* of experiment jobs, which bypasses the mount namespace. (3) CUDA and NVML need /sys, and a writable /sys/fs/cgroup view lets a jailed process write cgroup.freeze, memory.max or cpu.max of smatsprint-exp.slice, because the delegated subtree belongs to aurnab. (4) Without --clearenv, SSH_AUTH_SOCK, PYTHONPATH and the experiment's cache variables leak in from the invoking shell. (5) The viewer keeps the host network namespace, which shares every abstract Unix socket and every localhost port of the host. The sandbox shell's network is not specified.
findings.scenario: A sandbox trial hangs. The user opens sprintctl sbx shell, runs nvidia-smi, sees two python processes and runs kill -TERM on both. One was the experiment worker. It exits cleanly on SIGTERM, which R.2 does not restart, so the queue stops with no steering row and no ledger entry saying why. Variant: a sandbox script meant to cap its own memory writes memory.max at the wrong slice path, and the experiment's packed jobs die as host_oom.
findings.fix: Add to H.4 layer 1, after '--cap-drop ALL': '--unshare-pid, --unshare-ipc, --unshare-uts and --unshare-cgroup-try, with a fresh --proc /proc, so no experiment PID is visible or signalable; --ro-bind /sys /sys and never a writable /sys; --clearenv, then --setenv for an allow-list only (PATH, HOME, LANG, TMPDIR, the sandbox cache variables, CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, MUJOCO_GL); --unshare-net for every sandbox process, the shell included. The viewer also runs with --unshare-net. It listens on a Unix socket inside the sandbox tree, and a small unjailed forwarder in smatsprint-sbx.slice, with no other function and no file access, maps 127.0.0.1:8801 to that socket. jail.py builds this argument list and nothing else, and a unit test compares its argv with the list.'
findings.test: tests/lanes/test_escape_probes.py runs each probe inside the jail while the real tiny L0 pipeline runs, and every probe must fail: kill -0 and kill -STOP on the worker's host PID (taken from nvidia-smi and from the runner state); ls /proc/<worker pid> and readlink /proc/*/cwd; writing cgroup.freeze and memory.max under smatsprint-exp.slice; connecting to an abstract socket and to a 127.0.0.1 port opened by a test process outside the jail; env | grep SSH_AUTH_SOCK. After the probes, the worker's parameters at its next update equal those of a never-probed twin.

findings.where: H.4 layer 1 ('copy-in is done by the runner ... writes a read-only copy into the sandbox's copies/'); H.8 ('opened with O_NOFOLLOW'); H.4 layer 4 (write journal); H.7 (clean, idle stop); D.1 and D.2 (moving the sandbox tree); H.11 LI1 and LI6
findings.problem: The revision moved copy-in out of the jail. The runner, the most trusted writer and one that journals its own writes, now writes into copies/, a directory the sandbox controls. O_NOFOLLOW protects only the last path component of a Promote request. It does not stop a promote_outbox/ or copies/ directory that is itself a symlink, a hard link, or a file swapped between validation and registration. sbx clean, idle stop, the sandbox.json publisher and the move code also touch the sandbox tree from outside the jail, and none has a rule for opening paths there. A write that a planted link sends into the experiment tree goes through the journaling library, so the watcher of layer 4 sees a matching intent and stays silent. A hard link that already joins the two trees defeats the jail on its own. A jailed process can chmod u+w and rewrite the inode through its sandbox path, and inotify on the experiment directory never sees a write made through another directory's link.
findings.scenario: From a plain shell the user makes a convenience link: ln -s /home/aurnab/projects/smat-sprint/configs/registered copies/reg. Later, sprintctl sbx copy-in config smat-full@v3 --as reg/smat-full@v2.yaml makes the runner resolve the path, re-grant write permission as it does for its own writes, journal the intent, and overwrite a registered config. The watcher matches the journal entry and raises nothing. Only the next job's hash check (layer 3) notices, and the candidate refuses to run without an explanation.
findings.fix: Add H.4 layer 8: 'Unjailed code never follows the sandbox tree. Every component outside the jail that touches a sandbox path (Promote intake, copy-in, clean, idle stop, the sandbox.json publisher, moves) goes through lanes/sbxfs.py. It opens paths with openat2(RESOLVE_BENEATH | RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS | RESOLVE_NO_MAGICLINKS | RESOLVE_NO_XDEV) relative to a directory fd of the sandbox root. It accepts only regular files with st_nlink == 1, reads each one once into memory, and validates, hashes and registers from those bytes. The runner never writes inside the sandbox tree. Copy-in hands the bytes it read from the experiment to a jailed helper, which writes them with O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW into a new directory under copies/ as a full copy, never os.link, cp -l or rsync --link-dest. The write-journal library refuses any path whose resolved location differs from the path the caller named. The doctor and the jail launcher refuse to start any sandbox process while a file under the sandbox root shares (st_dev, st_ino) with a file under an experiment root.'
findings.test: At the paths each unjailed operation will touch, the fuzzer plants a symlinked copies/ and promote_outbox/, a hard link, a FIFO, a 2 GB file, and a file swapped between two reads (a rename race in a loop), then runs the operation. It asserts that no experiment file's bytes, mode or link count changed, that no write-journal entry for a sandbox operation names a path outside the sandbox tree, and that each case is refused with a plain reason.

findings.where: H.4 layer 4 (write journal) and LI10; C.2 layout (record state inside the dev tree); R.2 (unit table and watchdog list); N.8 (interactive sessions are not jailed)
findings.problem: Moving from process attribution (IM-15) to write intent was right, but the intent is unauthenticated. The journal is a file, and 'legitimate' means only that a write went through the shared library. So any process that imports the library counts as legitimate: a Codex session that 'fixes' a malformed row properly, a user's repair script, or the runner following a planted link (LI-02). The intent schema {path, new_sha256} cannot express deletions, renames, mode changes or new links. Nothing says what the 10-minute sweep compares against after downtime; if it is the watcher's own last manifest, the same user can edit that file. The watched 'experiment tree' is also the dev tree (C.2), where build sessions edit legitimately all day. Codex will likely exclude the dev tree to silence the noise, and configs/registered/ and ledger/ would be excluded with it. The watcher also has no unit and no heartbeat in R.2.
findings.scenario: The user opens an interactive Codex session to inspect a failed candidate. It runs outside any jail, because N.8 jails only wrapper sessions. It finds a result row with a missing field, imports smatsprint's ledger writer and rewrites the row 'correctly'. The library journals the intent, the watcher matches it, and the flag never rises.
findings.fix: Replace the second sentence of H.4 layer 4 with: 'Write intents are accepted only from the owner processes. The library sends each intent over a Unix socket in the record root, served by the watcher. The watcher reads the peer PID with SO_PEERCRED and accepts the intent only if /proc/<pid>/cgroup is exactly the cgroup of smatsprint-runner.service or smatsprint-controller.service, or a job scope that the worker registered with the watcher when it created it. The library refuses to write record state from any other cgroup, so a call from a Codex session or a shell fails loudly instead of being journaled. Intents cover create, write, rename, unlink, chmod and link. The sweep compares against the hashes the ledger recorded at registration or at DONE, plus the accepted intents, never against a manifest the watcher keeps. The watcher runs as smatsprint-lanewatch.service (enabled, Restart=always), its heartbeat is in the R.2 watchdog list, and no job is delivered while that heartbeat is stale.' In C.2, move record state out of the dev worktree (LI-04).
findings.test: LI10 as a black box. From a transient unit, a plain shell and an interactive codex exec session, call the project's own ledger and registration writers: each call is refused, and a direct file write is flagged within 60 s. An unlink, a rename-swap and a chmod on a registered config are each flagged. An edit made while the watcher is stopped is flagged before the next delivery.

findings.where: N.8 build jail ('read-write binds only for the dev tree, the sandbox tree ...'; 'SMATSPRINT_HOME read-only except the request spools'; '--ro-bind / /'; host network) and the launcher's named operations; C.2 layout; R.2 ('only the controller starts and stops' the worker); R.9
findings.problem: The new build jail keeps secrets out but does not keep the build away from the experiment lane. (1) C.2 still puts configs/registered/ and ledger/ in the dev tree (D.3 even tracks small ledger files on main), and the jail binds the dev tree read-write. A session can rewrite registered configs and ledger rows, or lose them to git stash -u, git checkout -- . or git reset --hard. A truncated ledger is still a valid chain, and N.8 itself calls the forbidden rules advice, not a lock. (2) The launcher installs unit files 'from a release tag', which the session itself creates. It also starts, stops or restarts any smatsprint-* unit. So session-written code can run outside the jail as a trusted unit, and the runner, worker or watcher can be stopped or restarted with no steering row, against R.2's rule that only the controller starts and stops the worker. (3) The sprintctl spool the session can write also carries sprintctl exp steering, so builder steering is logged as source cli, the same as the user's. (4) The sandbox tree is read-write for the session, so it can write promote_outbox/ (LI-06) or plant the links of LI-02. (5) --ro-bind / / keeps /tmp and /dev/shm from the host. connect() works through a read-only bind, so every Unix socket under /tmp, such as a forwarded ssh-agent, is reachable, and the host network adds every abstract socket. (6) Interactive sessions the user opens later are not jailed at all.
findings.scenario: During M4, while Q2 runs, a session adds a field to the result schema. It 'migrates' configs/registered/*.yaml in the dev tree and restarts smatsprint-runner through the launcher to pick up the change. Every candidate's registered hash now mismatches and every job refuses to start. If the session used the library, the watcher treats the rewrite as intended. No steering row explains any of it.
findings.fix: Add to C.2: 'Record state never lives in a git worktree. The record root is /home/aurnab/projects/smatsprint-record/ (ledger/, configs/registered/, state/, queue/, record/, work.d/). main tracks no ledger file. The ledger branch is built from a copy in a bare repository, as the status branch is.' Replace the read-write part of the N.8 bind list with: 'read-write binds only for the dev tree, which holds no record state, the project caches and ~/.codex; the sandbox tree and the record root read-only (the M3 day-one sandbox contents are written by a launcher operation); --tmpfs /tmp and --tmpfs /dev/shm. While the host network is used, no experiment-lane component listens on an abstract socket or a TCP port.' Replace the launcher's unit operations with: 'install unit files rendered from the templates in the current service tree, never from a session's tag; start or restart only the bridge, codexwrap and launcher units. The runner, controller, worker and watcher are stopped, restarted or released only through sprintctl drain and release (R.9), each logged as a steering row with source codex-build and the session number.' Add: 'The session's sprintctl spool accepts need and build commands only; steering from a build session is refused. Interactive Codex sessions run sprintctl build hold first (AGENTS.md) and start inside codexwrap/jail.py through sprintctl build shell.'
findings.test: M1 exit adds a build-lane canary, run inside the build jail. It writes to a registered config and to ledger/runs.jsonl, runs git stash -u and git reset --hard in the dev tree, sends sprintctl exp queue move, writes a promote_outbox file, asks the launcher to install a unit from a fresh tag and to restart smatsprint-worker, and connects to a socket under /tmp and to an abstract socket. Each attempt is refused or has no effect, and each refusal is logged. ss -xlp and ss -ltnp show no listener belonging to an experiment-lane unit.

findings.where: G.8 (gate-change refusal rule); D.3 ('Gate and tolerance changes never travel through the mailbox'); C.9 (an EVAL_HASH change re-evaluates claims); G.2 ('L3-provisional'); G.5 (held-out assets in criteria.yaml)
findings.problem: gate-change refuses a change only to a band 'that a claim with an existing result is judged on'. Results without a claim lock nothing: L3-provisional Stage-4 numbers, sweep members, screening pipelines and sandbox Stage-4 runs are all visible first. So a band can be widened after its numbers are known, whereas the request wants the bands fixed 'before any Stage 4 result is looked at'. Tightening is also allowed, and it can defeat a rival: narrowing the ±2 pp margin by which a velocity controller or B6 'does as well' keeps the method path open. The held-out asset lists in criteria.yaml (evaluation pool, partner seeds, replay data, Phase-2 start states) are neither bands nor thresholds, so gate-change can swap them freely. eval/ is a second route. A change there opens an evaluation epoch, and C.9 re-evaluates claims under the new definitions, so a claim can be re-judged by a metric redefined after its results were seen. IM-13 proposes showing both verdicts but does not say which one counts.
findings.scenario: Q4 finishes three L3-provisional pipelines with peak torque 0.72–0.74 against the band 0.83 ± 0.08, and no L3 claim exists yet. The user runs sprintctl gate-change l3.peak.halfwidth 0.12 --reason 'lighter device'. The change is accepted, and the next claim passes. Variant: a session changes the toe-off force threshold in eval/core from 5 % to 8 % of body weight. The new epoch re-evaluates the L1 claim, and it now passes.
findings.fix: Replace the refusal sentence in G.8 with: 'gate-change refuses any change, in either direction, to a band, threshold, margin or statistical rule once any experiment-lane row, claimed or not, provisional or screening, reports the metric that band reads for that level, or once the sandbox run index holds any result for that metric (an untrusted index can only lock a band, never unlock one). Held-out asset definitions (evaluation pools, partner seeds, replay data, Phase-2 start states) are immutable after the M1 freeze and have no gate-change key.' Add to C.9: 'A claim's verdict is its verdict under the evaluation epoch in force when the claim was created. Verdicts under later eval epochs are shown beside it and never turn a fail into a pass. An eval change that alters a gated metric on any stored result applies only to claims created after it.'
findings.test: Gate group: with only an L3-provisional row present, gate-change on the peak band is refused. A tightening after results exist is refused. A change to the partner seed list is refused. A synthetic eval epoch that would turn an L1 fail into a pass leaves the claim failed, with the later verdict shown beside it.

findings.where: H.8 (a request file in promote_outbox/ registers a candidate); H.3 (sandbox controls 'ask for nothing'); H.5 (reason and source); Page one ('Nothing invents or launches experiments on its own')
findings.problem: A Promote request is a file in a directory that the sandbox jail, build sessions (their jail binds the sandbox tree read-write) and any plain-shell process can all write. The runner cannot tell a request the user made from one a sandbox script wrote, so the one bridge has no authentication. A sandbox sweep script that ends with sprintctl sbx promote for each config it likes becomes an automatic proposer feeding the experiment queue. Its only limits are the schema and the cap of 20 pending requests, and its reason is whatever the script wrote.
findings.scenario: The user writes a sandbox loop that tries 40 observation variants overnight and promotes every variant whose sandbox symmetry beats 0.92. By morning 11 new experiment candidates are queued, each logged as a Promote with the reason 'auto', and they will run for days.
findings.fix: Replace the first paragraph of H.8 with: 'sprintctl sbx promote, inside the jail, only writes a promotion request. The request shows as pending on the Sandbox panel and in sprintctl exp promotions, and changes nothing. It becomes a candidate only when the user confirms it through the steering API: with the dashboard's Promote button, which sends a mailbox command carrying the request id and the validated diff shown to the user, or with sprintctl exp promote-confirm <request id> --reason <why> from an interactive SSH terminal. The CLI refuses confirmations that have no TTY or come from a sandbox, build or codex cgroup. At most promote_per_day confirmations are accepted (default 5), and requests expire after 7 days.'
findings.test: A script inside the jail that writes 30 requests registers no candidate. A confirmation from a process with no TTY, or from a smatsprint-build unit, is refused. A dashboard confirmation registers exactly the validated bytes that were shown, even if the sandbox file changed after validation.

findings.where: H.8 steps 1-3 ('the standard pipeline for its kind'; provenance); C.3 (symbolic parents); B.6 (B4 profile, B3 gains); the continuous parameters proposed in UX-04
findings.problem: Promote stops paths and checkpoints, but learned state can still cross as numbers or through the choice of parent. (a) If the schema allows arrays (a 101-point B4 phase profile, inline normalisation statistics, reward tables), a trained sandbox policy's torque curve or statistics cross as a 'config'. That is a result crossing, which H.8 forbids. (b) Baseline and ablation kinds branch from an experiment S2 checkpoint, and a symbolic parent lets the config choose which one. The sandbox can copy in every S2 checkpoint, find the S2 seed whose Stage 4 goes best, and promote a config pinned to it. (c) sandbox_diff and promoted_from come from sandbox-side metadata, which the user can edit. The provenance can say 'one weight changed' when ten fields changed, and it records nothing about the search that produced the config.
findings.scenario: The user extracts the mean exo torque curve from a sandbox Stage-4 checkpoint with a 12 % reduction and saves it as the B4 'fixed profile'. They promote it as a phase-profile baseline, and B4 in the experiment now replays a learned policy's output. Variant: they promote an ablation config whose symbolic parent is 'S2 of smat-full seed 402', chosen because that S2 gave the best Stage 4 in 15 sandbox trials.
findings.fix: Add to H.8 step 1: 'Values are scalars only, within their ranges and quantised to three significant figures. No array longer than 8 is allowed anywhere. Profiles, reference motions and normalisation statistics are referenced only by the id and hash of an asset in the experiment's own catalogue store, which Promote cannot write. A seed, a parent (symbolic or explicit) or a checkpoint selector is rejected. The parents of promoted baseline and ablation candidates are fixed by the paired-block rule of B.6 on seeds drawn at registration.' Replace the provenance in step 2 with: 'the runner itself computes sandbox_diff, field by field, between the promoted bytes and the experiment config the request names, which must exist in configs/registered/ or catalogue/. It adds, from the sandbox run index and labelled untrusted, the number of sandbox runs and evaluations in this config's lineage and the sandbox code identity they used.'
findings.test: Promote rejects a 101-float array, inline normaliser statistics, 'parent: S2 of seed 402' and 'seeds: [17]'. The recorded sandbox_diff equals the runner's own diff even when the request's metadata claims otherwise.

findings.where: H.1 and H.8 ('Nothing else crosses in that direction'); H.5 (cand edit --set, cand new --from, sweep launch); R.9 (catalogue releases); C.10 and C.14 (rows and the paper say whether a config came through Promote)
findings.problem: Promote is the only path that records sandbox provenance, but not the only way a sandbox-tuned value enters the experiment. The user can type the same values with cand edit --set, which is logged as an ordinary edit. A catalogue file added in a Codex session and released carries no provenance at all. A sweep can take the sandbox-tuned values as its options. So the 'came through Promote' flag, and the paper's statement about sandbox-derived configs, can be wrong through ordinary use.
findings.scenario: After 30 sandbox trials the user settles on h3d_phase, a log-std of -1.0 and a 1/1000 s timestep. Instead of Promote, they run sprintctl exp cand edit smat-full --set obs=h3d_phase --set logstd=-1.0 --set dt=0.001. The resulting L3 row says promoted: false.
findings.fix: Add to H.8: 'Every experiment registration (Promote, cand edit, cand new, a sweep member, a catalogue release) computes config_key, the sha256 of the canonical config with provenance, lane, name and version removed. It compares config_key, and the set of fields it changes, with the sandbox's config and run index, read through H.4 layer 8. An exact match is recorded on the candidate and on every row as sandbox_origin: <sandbox id> (suspected). The Ledger shows it, and the paper package lists the config as sandbox-derived. The catalogue is frozen with a manifest when the campaign starts. Entries added later carry origin: catalogue_post_m1 with the commit and the reason, and are treated like Promote.'
findings.test: Promote a config, then type its values with cand edit on another candidate: both rows carry sandbox provenance. A catalogue entry added after M1 carries catalogue_post_m1. The paper package's provenance table lists every suspected match.

findings.where: C.3 Seeds ('drawn per candidate from sha256(candidate_id)'); H.5 (an edit makes v+1 of the same candidate; cand new; Promote); R.3 Physics ('retry once ... with a new environment seed'); G.5
findings.problem: Training seeds belong to the candidate id, not the config, and they are derived from a string. So every version of a candidate reuses the same seeds, and editing v1 into v2 into v3 tunes the config to those seeds, which are then the seeds the claim is judged on. Re-adding the same catalogue entry, or promoting a config identical to an existing one, gets a new id and fresh seeds. That is seed re-rolling, and the discarded candidates never reach the gate. sha256 of a name can also be ground offline to land on seeds that trained well before, because a seed gives the same network initialisation across configs with the same architecture. R.3 retries a physics failure 'with a new environment seed', which quietly replaces a registered seed with one that works. The 900-949 overlap is IM-10 and the selection pool is UX-07.
findings.scenario: Candidate A's seed 1 falls in Stage 4, and the user kills A. They re-add the same catalogue entry as candidate B, which gets new seeds, and B's claim passes. A's failure stays in the ledger but never reaches the gate.
findings.fix: Replace the first sentence of C.3 'Seeds' with: 'Training seeds are drawn by the runner at registration from os.urandom, in 0-899. They are recorded in candidates.jsonl, never derived from a name, and fresh for every version. Seeds belong to config identity (config_key, H.8). check_gate.py judges a claim on the union of the registered seeds of every candidate version with the same config_key, including killed and failed ones. A seed killed before finishing counts as a failure unless it is requeued and finishes. A retried job keeps its environment seed. A retry that needs a new environment seed is a new attempt under the same (config_key, seed), and per-seed criteria use the first complete attempt.'
findings.test: Gate group: a claim whose killed sibling has the same config_key includes that sibling's failed seed and fails. v2's seeds are disjoint from v1's. A physics retry that succeeds with a new environment seed does not turn a failed seed into a pass.

findings.where: G.2 L3 and L4 (rival arms B0, B2, B4, B6); G.5 (a claim is created when a candidate first meets L1 or when the user registers a comparison; top-up seeds); H.5 (kill, pause and requeue of any candidate; stopping a sweep)
findings.problem: The spec never says what check_gate does when an arm of a registered claim is killed, paused, failed or still running. As a pure function it can make 'beats B2' vacuously true when B2 has no rows, and steering can kill or pause exactly the control that threatens a claim. A claim created when a candidate 'first meets L1' may register only the seeds that had finished, leaving out slower ones. Whether the 5 top-up seeds gate is open, so a verdict can depend on how many had finished by harvest time, which queue order and pauses control. A user-registered comparison lets the rival arms be picked after the results are known, for example the weakest B3 gain. A sweep stopped by steering while its current leader looks good is optional stopping.
findings.scenario: B2 is at 9 % on two of three seeds and SMAT is at 10 %. The user pauses B2 with the reason 'free the GPU for Phase 2'. Harvest re-evaluates the claim on the partial rows.
findings.fix: Add to G.5: 'When a claim is created it registers every seed its candidate has registered, finished or not, and states whether its top-ups gate (default: they are reported and never gate). check_gate.py returns pending until every gating arm has a complete result on every registered seed. A killed, paused, failed or missing arm keeps the claim incomplete; it never counts as a pass or a skip. The comparisons that can become claims are the contrasts pre-declared in gate/criteria.yaml (G.2, G.6, G.7, B.6) and user comparisons registered before any of their arms has a result at the compared stage. A comparison registered later is labelled post hoc and reaches only screening wording.' Add to H.5: 'Killing or pausing an arm of a registered claim is allowed, and the claim shows it with the steering action id. A sweep stopped early yields screening results only.'
findings.test: Gate group: a clean L4 ledger with B2's rows removed, killed or paused returns pending or incomplete, never pass. A claim created while 2 of 5 seeds are running includes all 5. A post-hoc comparison with a large effect fails the paper gate.

findings.where: H.7 copy-in allow-list ('excludes the held-out evaluation assets'); H.11 LI9; G.5; C.3 pools (sandbox evaluation seeds 20,000-20,999; no sandbox training pool)
findings.problem: The only thing keeping the sandbox from held-out assets is a copy-in allow-list, but those assets can be regenerated; they are not stored secrets. The held-out partners are seeds 900-949 run through the same code. CPU training is bit-reproducible, so a sandbox run with seed 905 and the catalogue config rebuilds partner 905 exactly. A device actor can then be tuned for cross-play against all 50 partners. Nothing requires a sandbox run to use the sandbox's own seed pools. The replay data is a public dataset, and any shell with network access can download it. LI9 ('never appear in the sandbox tree') would naturally be checked by path or name, which catches none of this.
findings.scenario: To improve partner transfer, the user runs S1 and S2 in the sandbox with seeds 900-909. The resulting humans are the held-out partners. A device actor tuned against them is promoted, and its L4(c) retention is inflated.
findings.fix: Add to H.7: 'Every seed a sandbox process uses goes through eval/core/seeds.py with lane=SANDBOX, which derives the generator state as the sha256 of the bytes SANDBOX followed by the seed. The same integer therefore gives different streams in the two lanes, and no sandbox run can reproduce an experiment policy, partner or evaluation episode. The sandbox API rejects seeds outside the sandbox pools (training 40,000-40,999, evaluation 20,000-20,999). Sandbox processes have no network (H.4 layer 1).' Replace LI9 with: 'No file under the sandbox tree has the sha256 of a held-out asset or of a checkpoint trained with a reserved seed. The doctor checks this daily by content, and copy-in checks it on every call.'
findings.test: A sandbox S1 run with integer seed 905 and the catalogue config produces weights whose hash differs from experiment partner 905's. A sandbox run with seed 900 or 10,001 is rejected. Planting the replay dataset in the sandbox tree under a new name trips LI9.

findings.where: C.2 (code_id from git tree hashes; run trees made with git archive; venv keyed by the uv.lock hash); H.4 layers 3 and 5; A.5 rule 5 (cache variables); R.2 (units)
findings.problem: A job runs much more than its hashes cover. (1) code_id hashes git objects, not the materialised run tree, and run trees are reused by code_id, so an in-place edit under work/code/<code_id>/ runs under an unchanged code_id. Python trusts a __pycache__ file whose header matches the source's mtime and size. An edit that keeps the file size, followed by touch -r, therefore runs edited bytecode while the source hash still verifies. git replace refs change what git archive extracts without changing any tree hash. (2) Venvs are identified only by the hash of uv.lock, and site-packages (torch, mujoco, myosuite, assist_sim) is never hashed. Unless UV_LINK_MODE=copy, uv links installed files to its cache, so two venvs built from one cache, which is tempting at 91 % disk use, can share files with the cache and with each other. Editable, path or .pth installs run code from outside the run tree. (3) Jobs take their environment from the user manager, which systemctl --user set-environment, ~/.config/environment.d and systemctl --user edit drop-ins change silently. PYTHONPATH, LD_PRELOAD, NVIDIA_TF32_OVERRIDE or CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG then change code or numerics without touching any watched file. (4) A process that misses one cache variable falls back to user-wide caches shared with plain-shell sandbox work and with the forge: ~/.cache/warp, /tmp/torchinductor_aurnab, ~/.triton and ~/.nv/ComputeCache.
findings.scenario: Testing a MyoSuite patch for the sandbox, the user edits a file in the sandbox venv from a plain shell. The file is shared with the experiment venv through the common uv cache. No watched directory sees the write, layer 3 checks no venv file, and every later Stage-1 job runs the patched MyoSuite under the same code_id.
findings.fix: Add to C.2: 'Each job records exec_id, the sha256 of four manifests. (1) The per-file manifest of its materialised run tree, verified at start against git ls-tree of its commit, with extraction under GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1. (2) The venv manifest: per-file sha256 of site-packages, excluding install metadata that embeds paths, written at build time, after which the venv is read-only. (3) The canonical job environment. (4) The unit files and drop-ins. Venvs are built with UV_LINK_MODE=copy from lane-specific uv caches, with no editable, path or .pth installs. Every job starts from env -i plus an allow-list built by the worker: every cache variable under the lane cache root, PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1, PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX set to a fresh per-job directory, and PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1. At start the job asserts that every module in sys.modules resolves under its run tree or its verified venv. Paired arms with different exec_id are not comparable.' Add to R.8: 'The doctor diffs systemctl --user show-environment, ~/.config/environment.d and the smatsprint drop-ins against the release manifest, and raises the modified-outside-the-steering-API flag on any drift.'
findings.test: Each of these is refused or flagged before the next job starts: an edit to a run-tree file followed by touch -r; a planted .pyc; git replace on a smatsprint/ blob; an edit to a venv file through a second link; systemctl --user set-environment NVIDIA_TF32_OVERRIDE=1; a drop-in that adds Environment=PYTHONPATH=; a job started with WARP_CACHE_PATH unset.

findings.where: H.4 layer 3 (the checked list: config, code_id, EVAL_HASH, GATE_HASH, parent checkpoint); C.3 job identity; C.5 (resume; DONE); D.5
findings.problem: Layer 3 checks each input's hash when the job starts, and the job then reopens the file by path. Nothing requires that the bytes hashed are the bytes used. safetensors files are usually memory-mapped, so an in-place write changes the tensors after the check. Python imports modules lazily for hours. Resume reloads 'the latest verified checkpoint' by path. The worker computes the DONE hashes by re-reading the files it wrote. Reference data is also missing from the list: every job loads the composed .mjb, the reference motion and the device model from work/refdata/, but none of them is in layer 3 or in job identity. A changed model or reference therefore runs unnoticed, and a requeued job can return a stored result computed on different data.
findings.scenario: A Stage-4 job verifies its parent S2 checkpoint and starts. Minutes later the human network is built from the memory-mapped safetensors, but by then the file has been rewritten in place through a hard link from the sandbox (LI-02). The job trains from weights other than the ones the ledger records.
findings.fix: Add to H.4 layer 3: 'Verify-then-use is one operation. The job reads each input once (config, parent checkpoint files, composed model, reference motion, device model) into its private run directory, hashes those bytes, writes them with O_EXCL and makes them read-only. It loads only the private copies, from memory, and never memory-maps a shared file. It imports every module before its first update. The model, reference and device hashes are part of job identity (C.3) and are checked against the hashes recorded at L0. The worker computes DONE hashes from the bytes it writes, in the same pass.'
findings.test: Crash-consistency group: a racing writer loop rewrites the parent checkpoint, the config, the .mjb and a lazily imported module from 1 ms to 10 minutes after job start. The job either refuses, or its trained parameters equal those of a race-free twin. A rollout changed between its write and DONE fails the record copy.

findings.where: C.5 packer ('free minus 10 %'); H.4 layer 6; R.2 host fence (MemoryHigh=17G on smatsprint.slice); R.5 (progress-watchdog strikes); G.7 benchmark path
findings.problem: Sharing resources with the sandbox can change verdicts, not only wall-clock times. The world-count fallback is covered by SM-23 and contention with the forge by SM-09 and SM-10; these gaps are specific to the sandbox. (1) The packer does not reserve the sandbox's VRAM cap. An experiment GPU job admitted while the sandbox is idle hits out-of-memory when the sandbox later grows, still within its 4 GB. (2) PyTorch's per-process memory fraction does not cover Warp or MuJoCo Warp allocations or the CUDA context. The NVML watchdog allows up to 15 s over the cap, so the sandbox's VRAM cap is weaker than stated. (3) Sandbox runs follow no MemAvailable admission rule and have no OOM priority, so the kernel's global OOM killer can pick an experiment environment process. The MemoryHigh on the parent smatsprint.slice throttles experiment allocations whenever the sandbox pushes the parent past 17 GB. (4) GPU time-slicing and CPU contention (no cpuset; shared SMT siblings, L3 cache and memory bandwidth) slow experiment jobs. R.5 counts a progress-watchdog event as a strike, and the throughput the benchmark path publishes is measured under a sandbox load that nobody records.
findings.scenario: A 4,096-world Stage-1 GPU job is admitted with 5 GB of headroom. An hour later the user starts a 2,048-world sandbox trial within the 4 GB cap. The experiment job hits out-of-memory repeatedly, and each resume fails again until the user closes the sandbox.
findings.fix: Add to C.5: 'While the sandbox slice exists, the packer reserves the sandbox's full VRAM and RAM caps. The sandbox API admits a run only if every admitted experiment job's reservation stays intact.' Add to R.2: 'Sandbox units get OOMScoreAdjust=1000 and their own MemoryHigh. smatsprint.slice has no MemoryHigh of its own. The sandbox follows the worker's MemAvailable admission rule.' Add to R.5: 'A progress-watchdog event while the sandbox or the forge used more than 25 % of the GPU or of the lane's CPU is an infrastructure event, not a strike.' Add to C.10: 'Throughput and wall-clock rows record the sandbox's and the forge's GPU and CPU use during the job. Only calibration jobs run with the sandbox stopped feed a throughput claim.'
findings.test: GPU fixtures: the sandbox grows to its cap during an experiment job, and the job continues or waits with no strike. A sandbox run that would breach an admitted reservation is refused. A memory hog in the sandbox slice never causes an OOM kill in smatsprint-exp.slice. A throughput job run while the sandbox is active is excluded from the benchmark claim.

findings.where: A.5 rule 5 (one 30 GB cap for both lanes; min_free_gb 65; hard_floor_gb 55); R.3 Disk; H.7; H.11 fuzzer ('fill the disk of the sandbox tree')
findings.problem: The two lanes share one filesystem and one 30 GB cap, and neither lane has a quota, because quotas need root. Sandbox trials, render loops or copy-ins can push free space below min_free_gb, where the experiment starts nothing new, or below hard_floor_gb, where it goes to SAFE_PAUSE. R.3 prunes only experiment files. So a sandbox action changes the experiment's job state, and the fuzzer's own assertion after it fills the sandbox disk will fail, while the spec never says how to prevent that.
findings.scenario: Overnight the user leaves a render loop running with three 5 M trials that save rollouts. Free space falls from 67 GB to 54 GB, and at 03:00 the experiment goes to SAFE_PAUSE and waits for a person.
findings.fix: Add to H.7: 'The sandbox has its own disk budget (default 8 GB, inside the programme cap). The sandbox API checks it before every run, render and copy-in. The sandbox watchdog checkpoints and stops sandbox processes when the tree exceeds its budget or when shared free space falls below min_free_gb + 5 GB, so the sandbox always stops before the experiment reaches its floor. R.3 prunes sandbox clips, runs and copies older than sandbox_keep_days first, after a sandbox_disk need that shows the sizes.'
findings.test: Fuzzer: filling the sandbox tree to the stop threshold stops the sandbox and leaves the experiment RUNNING with its queue unchanged. The same fill with the sandbox watchdog disabled makes the test fail, which proves the test can see it.

findings.where: H.4 layer 3 (chain verified at start and every 10 minutes); R.7; D.3 ruleset A (the deploy key is the bypass actor on every branch except control); D.8 deadman.yml
findings.problem: A hash chain only proves that its rows agree with each other. A process running as the same user, or anyone holding the deploy key, can drop or edit rows and then recompute the whole chain, and a truncated ledger is still a valid chain. The GitHub copy does not help. Ruleset A lets the deploy key update any branch, force-pushes included, and nothing checks that each new ledger commit only appends to the previous one.
findings.scenario: After a disappointing L3 result, the user runs a small script that deletes the row of the seed that fell, recomputes the chain, and force-pushes the ledger branch with the deploy key. The runner's chain check passes, and check_gate now sees three passing seeds.
findings.fix: Add to R.7: 'The runner keeps the ledger head (row count and last row hash) in state/ledger_head.json and in every status.json. It refuses to start, and raises the flag, when the ledger is shorter than the recorded head or does not extend it. Before every commit it verifies that the new runs.jsonl and steering.jsonl extend the previous commit's files byte for byte.' Add to D.3: 'Ruleset C on the ledger branch blocks non-fast-forward pushes and deletion, with no bypass actor, the deploy key included.' Add to D.8: 'deadman.yml also checks that the ledger files at the branch head extend those at the last verified commit. It records each verified head as a comment on a pinned issue, and opens an alert issue if the ledger shrank or its history was replaced.'
findings.test: Three tampering cases, each either refused or detected within one runner cycle and one workflow run: truncating the last row; rewriting a middle row and recomputing the chain; force-pushing from a clone with the deploy key.

findings.where: D.3 Writing (inbox {id, command, args, reason, based_on, created_at, client}); D.3 threat model; H.5; H.8 (the dashboard's Promote button); SM-22 (shared Pages origin)
findings.problem: The mailbox authenticates a token, not a person or a device. The client field is self-reported, and every device posts as the same GitHub user, so steering done with a leaked token is logged exactly like the user's own. D.3 limits what a stolen token can spend, but not what it can do to the evidence. It can Promote any sandbox config, kill or pause claim arms, edit candidates, add post-hoc seeds, launch sweeps and change the lane split. Every later result then lists 'the steering actions that preceded it' as if the user had chosen them. SM-22 describes how a token can leak through the shared Pages origin.
findings.scenario: A token is read from the shared origin's storage. The attacker, or a buggy script that reuses the token, sends cand kill for B2 and B6 of an L4 claim and then a Promote. The Ledger shows all three as the user's, sent from 'phone'.
findings.fix: Add to D.3 'Dashboard auth': 'At device registration the page creates a non-extractable ECDSA P-256 key with WebCrypto and keeps it in IndexedDB. register_device carries the public key, and the registration takes effect only after the owner taps Confirm on a Telegram need that names the device. Each later inbox command is signed with that key over (id, command, args, reason, based_on, created_at). The controller rejects any command that is unsigned or signed by an unconfirmed key, and records the device id in the steering row. Pause and emergency stop are exempt, so they always work.'
findings.test: Playwright and state-machine tests: a well-formed command sent with a valid token but no signature is rejected. A command signed by a registered but unconfirmed key is rejected. A device confirmed through the fake Telegram backend succeeds, and the steering row names it.

findings.where: C.1 (the worker runs training, evaluations and renders on Vast); C.4 harvest (metrics from saved rollouts); D.2 move_to_lab step 2 (rsync from the worker to staging); D.5 ('anything that has been on a rented host is untrusted data'); R.10; G.6 G5
findings.problem: D.5 declares data returning from Vast untrusted, but the spec then harvests it as a first-class result. (1) Evaluation jobs may run on Vast, and the runner computes the gated metrics from rollouts the rented host wrote. A faulty or hostile host can produce plausible rollouts that pass L3, and G5's second-machine replication runs entirely there. (2) move_to_lab copies the worker's whole work state back into a lab generation, because only move_to_vast excludes code/ and compile_cache/. Warp, Triton and Inductor caches (compiled .so and .cubin files), __pycache__ and run trees written on the rented host can therefore come home and be loaded by lab jobs, which R.10 forbids. (3) work/refdata/ coming back from Vast is checked only against a manifest the same host wrote.
findings.scenario: A Vast host with faulty memory writes subtly corrupted rollouts that still parse. The runner computes an 11 % reduction for an arm the lab would put at 7 %, and the claim passes G1 and G5 on that host's data alone.
findings.fix: Add to C.4: 'Every gating metric comes from an evaluation run on the lab; Vast runs training only. Before any gate reads a stage-final checkpoint trained on Vast, the lab re-evaluates it. For one update per Vast-trained stage, the lab also replays the update from the mirrored checkpoint and compares the resulting parameters within the backend tolerance. A mismatch quarantines every row from that host.' Add to D.2 move_to_lab step 2: 'exclude work/code/, work/compile_cache/, every __pycache__ and every cache directory; the lab regenerates them. Verify work/refdata/ against the hashes recorded at L0, never against a manifest from the worker.'
findings.test: Migration rehearsal: a fake worker returns a rollout with inflated activations, a .so file in compile_cache/ and a modified refdata file. The claim is computed from the lab re-evaluation, the .so never reaches a lab generation, and the refdata mismatch refuses the move.

findings.where: H.9 ('build the runner for their materials when they exist'); D.5 ('checkpoints are never pickles'); C.10 and G.7 (independent-reconstruction claims)
findings.problem: Exact replay keeps its rows apart, but not the author materials or what they reveal. (1) The authors' checkpoints are most likely Stable-Baselines3 zips, which contain pickles. The replay runner is to be built later, inside the experiment lane, where unpickling would run arbitrary code as the experiment worker with write access to record state. (2) Once the authors' code is on the lab, their observation order, normalisation and reference file can reach the 'independent' reconstruction through ordinary edits, and the rows would still be labelled independent. (3) Author files placed in work/refdata/ could become the parent, reference or normaliser of a reconstruction candidate.
findings.scenario: The authors send SMAT-Exo. The user reads their environment code and, with cand edit, sets the observation order and normalisation statistics to theirs. The resulting L3 claim is written up as an independent reconstruction.
findings.fix: Replace the last sentence of H.9 with: 'Author materials are untrusted input. They are unpacked and converted only inside a jail of their own (the H.4 layer-1 recipe, with a replay tree and no network). There, pickles are loaded and re-saved as safetensors and JSON. Only the converted, hashed files enter the experiment, tagged source: author. Nothing tagged source: author may be the parent, reference, normaliser or model of a reconstruction candidate. When materials arrive the runner records author_materials_at. Every candidate registered after that carries informed_by_author_materials: true and is never called an independent reconstruction.'
findings.test: A replay zip whose pickle writes a file runs only inside the replay jail, and the file never appears in the experiment tree. A candidate registered after author_materials_at is labelled informed. A job whose parent hash matches a file tagged source: author is refused.

findings.where: H.2 roots (/home/aurnab/projects/smat-sprint/ and /home/aurnab/projects/smat-sprint-sandbox/); H.11 LI1, LI5 and LI10; H.4 layers 1 and 4
findings.problem: The experiment root is a string prefix of the sandbox root, so any containment check written with startswith treats sandbox files as experiment files. That mistake is easy to make in the LI5 checker, the edit and Promote validators, the jail's bind builder and the watcher's scope. An experiment job can then reference a sandbox checkpoint while passing a 'must be under the experiment root' check, or the watcher can watch the wrong tree.
findings.scenario: cand edit --set init_from=/home/aurnab/projects/smat-sprint-sandbox/runs/sbx_12/ckpt passes startswith('/home/aurnab/projects/smat-sprint'), and a checkpoint trained in the sandbox becomes the parent of an experiment stage.
findings.fix: In H.2, rename the roots so that no root is a prefix of another: /home/aurnab/projects/smatsprint-exp/ for the code and service trees, /home/aurnab/projects/smatsprint-record/ for record state (LI-04), and /home/aurnab/projects/smatsprint-sbx/ for the sandbox. Add to H.4: 'Every containment check resolves both paths and compares them with Path.is_relative_to. A grep test bans startswith on path strings.'
findings.test: Unit tests cover the sibling-prefix, trailing-slash, .. and symlink cases for every containment helper. A grep test finds no startswith applied to a path in lanes/, runner/ or control/.

findings.where: C.7 ('the selection rule, chosen from the fixed library in runner/rules.py with its parameters, all hashed'); C.3 (symbolic parents resolved by a declared rule); R.9; C.2 (code_id covers only smatsprint/, eval/ and uv.lock)
findings.problem: A sweep hashes its rule's id and parameters, but the code that evaluates the rule lives in runner/rules.py. That file is outside code_id, EVAL_HASH and GATE_HASH, and any release can change it. The symbolic-parent resolver has the same problem. A release made after the members' results are visible can therefore change which member an already-registered sweep selects, or which S2 checkpoint becomes a parent, without touching the sweep's registration.
findings.scenario: A sweep's rule, 'L1 pass count, then symmetry deficit', picks config 7. A session 'fixes' rules.py so that ties break on speed error first, and releases it. Config 12 is now selected and promoted to P3 on fresh seeds.
findings.fix: Add to C.7: 'The selection-rule library and the symbolic-parent resolver live in gate/rules/ and are covered by GATE_HASH. A sweep records the gate epoch it was registered under, and its selections are always computed with that epoch's rules. A rule change opens a gate epoch (G.8) and applies only to sweeps registered after it.'
findings.test: Gate group: changing a rule's tie-break after a sweep's members finish leaves that sweep's selection unchanged, while a sweep registered after the change uses the new rule.

findings.where: H.11 (the fuzzer and the acceptance rehearsal); E.2 Lanes group
findings.problem: From inside the jail, where the experiment paths are not mounted, the fuzzer tries to write, rename, symlink, hard-link and chmod experiment files. Every attempt fails with ENOENT, which proves nothing. It uses a dummy job that has none of the real worker's shared memory, open descriptors or GPU context. It never attacks from where leaks actually come: signals, /proc, cgroupfs and sockets (LI-01); the unjailed components that read the sandbox tree (LI-02); write-library calls from other cgroups (LI-03); build sessions (LI-04); the venv and the environment (LI-12). The acceptance rehearsal performs only legitimate actions.
findings.scenario: The fuzzer passes 10,000 steps even though the jail shares the host PID namespace, because none of its actions is kill.
findings.fix: Replace the fuzzer paragraph of H.11 with: 'The fuzzer runs against the real worker on the tiny L0 pipeline (CPU environment pool with shared memory, plus a GPU job once M4 exists), with the watcher running. Its actions are: the LI-01 escape probes; the LI-02 plants, each followed by the unjailed sandbox operation it targets; write-library calls from foreign cgroups; the LI-04 build-lane canary; the LI-12 edits to the venv, the environment and __pycache__; resource hogs at and above every cap; seed-regeneration attempts (LI-11); and every sandbox command and Promote with valid and hostile inputs. After every step it asserts LI1-LI10, the exec_id, the ledger head, and parameters bit-equal to a never-fuzzed twin at the next update.'
findings.test: Mutation check: run the fuzzer against a deliberately weakened build (no --unshare-pid, a writable cgroupfs, a watcher that accepts intents from any cgroup). It must fail within its default budget. A fuzzer that stays green against the weakened build is itself a red test.

findings.where: C.10 (equal budgets); C.4 harvest; B.2 physics audit (run in the worker)
findings.problem: Metrics are recomputed from rollouts, but the facts behind equal budgets come from the worker's results.json: transitions per stage, per-actor update counts, and the torque limit, which the worker asserts against the configured scale. So a config mistake or a worker bug passes the matched-budget check.
findings.scenario: A variant sets the Stage-4 torque scale to 30 Nm through a mis-keyed field. The worker's audit bounds forces by the configured 30 Nm and passes, and the comparison with SMAT at 25 Nm is labelled matched.
findings.fix: Add to C.4 harvest: 'The runner derives transitions from curves.csv (updates times the registered batch geometry) and cross-checks them with results.json. It derives the applied torque bound from the evaluation rollouts (the maximum |tau| per stage) and compares it with the stage scale in gate/criteria.yaml, not with the config. A mismatch labels the row not comparable.'
findings.test: Synthetic records: a results.json claiming 66 M transitions whose curves show 33 M is labelled not comparable, and so is a rollout that reaches 30 Nm in a 25 Nm arm.

findings.where: H.7 sbx compare; D.4 Sandbox panel; H.8 Promote dialog
findings.problem: sbx compare computes the G.3 metrics with the sandbox's own code, which the user may have edited, and shows them beside the experiment's numbers. Nothing says whether that code matches EVAL_HASH. A sandbox number that looks like a reproduction may come from a changed metric, and the user then decides to Promote on a false premise.
findings.scenario: To debug gait events, the user changes the toe-off threshold in the sandbox copy of eval/core and forgets to change it back. Compare shows toe-off at 58 %. The config is promoted, and the experiment reports 64 %.
findings.fix: Add to H.7: 'Every sandbox metric carries the sandbox's eval hash. When it differs from EVAL_HASH, compare, the Sandbox panel and the Promote dialog show in amber: metric code differs from the experiment's.'
findings.test: Change one line of the sandbox's eval/core, then check with Playwright that compare, the Sandbox panel and the Promote dialog all show the warning.

findings.where: H.5 (pause, resume, edit, requeue); C.3 job identity
findings.problem: The spec does not say which version a paused candidate resumes as after an edit, or whether a new version may continue from an older version's intermediate checkpoint. An implementation that finds 'the candidate's job' by candidate id would continue v1's half-trained stage under v2's config, producing a hybrid run recorded under v2's hash.
findings.scenario: The user pauses smat-full during S1, edits the entropy coefficient to make v2, and resumes. S1 continues from v1's checkpoint at update 400 with v2's settings.
findings.fix: Add to H.5: 'Pause and resume act on jobs, not candidates. A resumed job keeps its identity and its version. An edit never affects a paused, running or partly run job. The jobs of version v+1 start from their stages' registered parents, never from an intermediate checkpoint of version v.'
findings.test: Pause, edit, resume: the resumed job's config hash is still v1's, and v2's S1 job starts at update 0.

strengths: Promote carries one config and never a checkpoint or a result; the candidate trains from scratch, and the validator rejects paths, init_from, result references and unknown keys. The revised intake opens the request with O_NOFOLLOW, accepts regular files up to 64 kB only, and never executes or imports it.

Layer 4 moved from process attribution, which cannot be built without root, to write intents plus a full hash sweep at every start. That is the right direction and covers the watcher's downtime in principle.

The sandbox jail now hides /run/user/<uid>, which closes the systemd-run --user escape, uses a private /tmp and /dev/shm, and drops all capabilities. Copy-in moved out of the jail and is checked against an allow-list.

The build jail uses --unshare-pid with a fresh /proc, puts tmpfs over other projects' secrets and hides the user bus. Its launcher runs named operations only, never a command string, and M0 canaries test it.

Steering cannot change eval/ or gate/, cannot delete or hide rows, and cannot edit a running job. An edit creates a new version. A sweep's space, rule, budget and seeds are frozen at its first job. A budget change to one arm of a paired block is refused.

Post-hoc seeds are recorded as such and never gate. A claim's statement, arms, metrics and seeds freeze when it is created, and a changed statement is a new claim that leaves the old verdict standing.
Harvest recomputes every metric from saved rollouts with frozen eval/core instead of trusting the worker's numbers, and every reported metric is measured on the CPU reference physics.

Registered configs are versioned, read-only and hash-checked at job start, together with code_id, EVAL_HASH, GATE_HASH and the parent checkpoint. Job identity is content-based, and a science-code release gives new candidates a new code_id without touching old ones.
Gate changes happen only over SSH, open a visible and alerted epoch, and never travel through the mailbox or Telegram.
The lanes have separate slices, caches and a sandbox evaluation seed pool. An out-of-memory caused by sandbox growth adds no strike. The sandbox stays on the lab unless the user ticks the box.
Every result carries its lane, its steering references and its Promote provenance, and the paper package is built only from the ledger.
Checkpoints are never pickles (safetensors and JSON, enforced by a grep test), which closes code-in-checkpoint channels between the lanes.
